muc.title: Newer isn't always a better fit
muc.text: An AI company just released a new model, faster and cheaper. The bank's chatbot team wants to switch right away. Wait. Newer isn't always a better fit.

muc.title: The product's own test
muc.text: They already have a test set, called an eval set: a few hundred real customer questions with the answers they want, plus trick questions they've seen before.

muc.title: Old and new take the test
muc.text: The new model has to redo the whole old test, and its score is compared with the model that's running now. This is called a regression test.

muc.title: AI grades, people check
muc.text: Grading hundreds of answers by hand takes a long time, so they use an AI as the judge, called LLM as a judge, grading against clear criteria. Then people double-check the hard ones.

muc.title: Better overall, worse where it matters
muc.text: The results can be surprising: the new model does better on ninety questions, but worse on five about annual fees. Until those five are fixed, no switch.

muc.title: Change anything, test again
muc.text: It's not just switching models. Changing one word in the prompt or adding a document also means testing again. Unlike the benchmarks in the grading series, this eval set belongs to that product alone.

muc.title: Five questions of your own
muc.text: When an AI app you use gets a new model, take five questions of your own, like in video 48. Ask both the old and new model, and compare before switching for good.

muc.title: When things go wrong, how do you trace it?
muc.text: The switch is done, and it's live. If something goes wrong, how do you trace it? Part six: logging and tracing.
